title: Episode 300: Henry III: The Barons' War, Simon de Montfort, and the First English Parliament
description:
The monumental, pious, and stormy fifty-six-year reign of King Henry III: the nine-year-old boy king who inherited an England torn apart by civil war and French invasion, and grew into a deeply religious patron of the arts who rebuilt Westminster Abbey in magnificent Gothic splendor. Devoted to the cult of Edward the Confessor, Henry's lavish spending on Italian papal adventures and his favoritism toward foreign Lusignan and Savoyard relatives provoked a furious baronial revolution. Led by his own brother-in-law, the fiery crusader Simon de Montfort, the barons imposed the Provisions of Oxford in 1258. Culminating in the Battle of Lewes, the summoning of the historic 1265 Parliament with elected borough burgesses, and de Montfort's slaughter at Evesham, discover the birth of Parliament.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series reaches our milestone three-hundredth episode, exploring the dramatic fifty-six-year reign of Henry III: the pious builder of Westminster Abbey whose clash with Simon de Montfort created the world's first representative parliament. Here is George with the extraordinary life of King Henry III.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE BOY KING AND THE GREATEST KNIGHT: 1216 TO 1227
Born in October 1207 at Winchester, Henry was just nine years old when his hated father King John died in October 1216, leaving the English kingdom half-conquered by Prince Louis of France and rebel barons. In a hasty, improvised ceremony at Gloucester Cathedral on October 28, 1216, young Henry was crowned with his mother Queen Isabella's gold circlet, because his father had lost the crown jewels in the Wash. The survival of the child king was an epic triumph of one man's chivalric honor: seventy-year-old William Marshal, 1st Earl of Pembroke—universally revered as 'the greatest knight that ever lived'—accepted the regency of the realm. Marshal defeated the French at the Battle of Lincoln in 1217, reissued Magna Carta with the Great Seal, and expelled the foreign invaders, handing eighteen-year-old Henry a unified and peaceful kingdom upon his death.  The survival of the child King Henry III in the dark autumn of 1216 was an extraordinary miracle of medieval chivalry: with Prince Louis of France occupying London and Winchester and half the English barons in open rebellion, seventy-year-old William Marshal took the weeping nine-year-old boy by the hand, declaring to the assembled knights: 'Behold your king!' Marshal's decisive victory at the Battle of Lincoln in May 1217—a savage street-by-street melee known as 'the Fair of Lincoln'—smashed the French invasion, while Hubert de Burgh's naval victory off Dover destroyed the French relief fleet. By reissuing Magna Carta in 1217 and 1225 with the Great Seal, William Marshal and the regency council saved the Plantagenet crown, cementing the Great Charter as the permanent statutory law of England.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SPLENDOR OF GOTHIC WESTMINSTER: 1245 TO 1269
Henry III was an aesthetically sensitive, deeply cultured sovereign whose piety was the defining passion of his existence: he attended Mass three times a day, wept when touching holy relics, and adopted Edward the Confessor as his personal patron saint, naming his eldest son Edward in his honor. In 1245, Henry embarked on his supreme architectural masterpiece: demolishing Edward the Confessor's Romanesque church at Westminster to construct the breathtaking Gothic abbey that stands today. Inspired by the soaring French cathedrals of Amiens and Sainte-Chapelle, Henry imported master masons and Italian Cosmati mosaicists, constructing soaring pointed arches, delicate stone tracery, and the magnificent Cosmati pavement before the high altar, pouring over forty thousand silver pounds into the golden shrine of Saint Edward.  Henry III's obsession with Westminster Abbey transformed the English royal court into a dazzling center of European high Gothic art and culture: the king spent over forty-five thousand pounds—the equivalent of an entire year of national royal revenue—importing fine Caen stone from Normandy, marble from the Isle of Purbeck, and master Roman mosaicists from the Cosmati workshops. The magnificent Cosmati pavement laid before the high altar, crafted from geometric discs of porphyry, serpentine, and colored glass, was designed as a mystical map of the universe, calculating the exact duration of the cosmos until the Day of Judgment. In October 1269, in an ecstatic display of personal piety, King Henry, his brother Richard of Cornwall, and his two sons carried the golden, jewel-encrusted coffin of Saint Edward the Confessor upon their shoulders, placing it in the magnificent shrine behind the high altar.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE ALIEN FAVORITES AND THE SICILIAN BLUNDER: 1236 TO 1258
Despite his artistic brilliance, Henry was an incompetent political manager: impulsive, easily manipulated, and lacking fiscal discipline. In 1236, Henry married Eleanor of Provence, opening the floodgates to hundreds of foreign relatives: Eleanor's Savoyard uncles were showered with bishoprics and earldoms, while Henry's French half-brothers from Poitou—the arrogant Lusignans—were granted vast estates and acted above the law. Henry's folly reached its zenith in 1254 in the 'Sicilian Business': Pope Innocent IV offered the vacant crown of Sicily to Henry's eight-year-old second son Edmund, on the condition that Henry finance a papal army to conquer it from the Hohenstaufens. Henry recklessly agreed to pay the astronomical sum of one hundred and thirty-five thousand silver marks—an impossible debt that brought England to the verge of national bankruptcy and provoked a baronial revolt.  Henry's generous, affectionate nature was exploited by foreign courtiers who treated the English treasury as an open trough: his wife's Savoyard relatives, led by Peter of Savoy and Boniface of Savoy—whom Henry appointed Archbishop of Canterbury—monopolized crown patronage, while Henry's Poitevin half-brothers, the Lusignans, rode through the countryside assaulting royal bailiffs and boasting that the king's law did not apply to them. Henry's catastrophic 'Sicilian Business' in 1254 was a masterpiece of geopolitical naivety: seduced by Pope Innocent IV's promise of the Sicilian crown for young Prince Edmund, Henry agreed to bankroll a papal military expedition to conquer southern Italy. When the crushing debt of one hundred and thirty-five thousand marks threatened to bankrupt the kingdom, the English Church and baronage erupted in furious mutiny.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE PROVISIONS OF OXFORD: ENGLAND'S FIRST WRITTEN CONSTITUTION: 1258
In April 1258, a delegation of seven major barons strode into the royal hall at Westminster Palace clad in full battle chainmail, their swords rattling in their scabbards. A terrified King Henry stammered: 'What is this, my lords? Am I your prisoner?' Earl Roger Bigod replied: 'No, Sir King, but your foreign favorites must be banished and the realm reformed.' In June 1258, the barons met at Oxford, compelling Henry to accept the revolutionary 'Provisions of Oxford'—England's first written constitution. The Provisions placed the sovereign under the control of an elected Council of Fifteen barons, mandated that Parliament meet three times a year, expelled the hated Lusignans, and placed sheriffs and the treasury under baronial oversight, stripping the monarchy of absolute power.  The revolutionary assembly at Oxford in June 1258, known to history as the 'Mad Parliament', was a watershed moment in constitutional development: the barons, led by Simon de Montfort, compelled King Henry to swear on the Holy Gospels to accept the Provisions of Oxford. This historic document established an elected Council of Fifteen magnates without whose consent the king could make no decisions, created an independent Chancellor and Treasurer responsible to the council, mandated that Parliament assemble three times a year regardless of the king's wishes, and required all royal officials to swear an oath to the community of the realm rather than the person of the monarch, transforming England into a constitutional baronial republic.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: SIMON DE MONTFORT AND THE BATTLE OF LEWES: MAY 14, 1264
The undisputed leader of the baronial revolution was Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester: a brilliant Anglo-French nobleman, seasoned crusader, and the husband of King Henry's sister Eleanor. De Montfort was a fiery idealist who wore hairshirts beneath his armor, viewed the Provisions of Oxford as a sacred holy covenant, and possessed a charismatic moral fervor that rallied university scholars, London merchants, and lesser knights to his cause. When King Henry obtained a papal bull from Rome releasing him from his oaths and repudiated the Provisions, civil war—the Second Barons' War—erupted. On May 14, 1264, on the chalk downs of Lewes in Sussex, de Montfort's smaller army outmaneuvered the royalists. Henry III and his formidable son Prince Edward were captured on the field, leaving Simon de Montfort as the uncrowned ruler of England.  The civil war that erupted in 1264 pit brother-in-law against brother-in-law: Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester, was a towering military genius whose deep religious convictions convinced him that resisting an oath-breaking king was a sacred Christian duty. At the Battle of Lewes on May 14, 1264, de Montfort's rebel army, wearing white crosses on their chests like crusaders, deployed on the crest of the Sussex downs. When Prince Edward led a reckless cavalry charge that routed de Montfort's London allies and chased them for miles, de Montfort seized the center, smashing King Henry's remaining forces. When Prince Edward returned to the battlefield, he found his father a captive inside Lewes Priory, forcing both king and prince to surrender as prisoners of war.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE 1265 PARLIAMENT: THE BIRTH OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS: JANUARY 1265
Ruling England with the puppet King Henry in his custody, Simon de Montfort made an epoch-defining political innovation. In January 1265, seeking to broaden his political legitimacy beyond the fractious aristocracy, de Montfort summoned a national assembly to Westminster Palace. For the first time in world history, the summons went out not merely to the great earls, bishops, and two knights from each shire, but explicitly demanded the election of two burgesses—two ordinary citizens—from every major city and borough in England. In this humble gathering of knights and merchants seated alongside peers in the Chapter House of Westminster, the modern House of Commons was born, establishing the foundational principle of representative democracy: that those who pay taxes to the state must have an elected voice in governing the nation.  In January 1265, ruling England from London with the captive king as an ornamental figurehead, Simon de Montfort made the revolutionary political decision that birthed the modern democratic state. Recognizing that he needed the financial support and political legitimacy of the emerging merchant and gentry classes, de Montfort summoned two knights from every shire and two burgesses from every chartered borough to attend Parliament alongside the great earls and bishops. Meeting in the Chapter House of Westminster Abbey, this gathering of common citizens alongside noble peers established the foundational principle that the ordinary people of England—the 'Commons'—held an inalienable right to debate taxation, petition grievances, and participate in national legislation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BLOOD OF EVESHAM AND THE REBURIAL OF THE CONFESSOR: 1265 TO 1272
De Montfort's parliamentary republic was brief and bloody: in May 1265, nineteen-year-old Prince Edward escaped captivity by exhausting his guards' horses in races, mobilizing a royalist army in the Welsh borders. On August 4, 1265, in a ferocious thunderstorm at the Battle of Evesham in Worcestershire, Prince Edward trapped de Montfort's outnumbered force in a bend of the River Avon. Seeing the royalist banners advance, de Montfort famously whispered: 'May the Lord have mercy on our souls, for our bodies are theirs!' De Montfort was hacked down, his body brutally mutilated, his head severed and paraded on a spear. King Henry III was rescued from the melee and restored to his throne. In October 1269, Henry fulfilled his life's sacred dream, carrying the coffin of Saint Edward on his shoulders into his completed Gothic Westminster Abbey. Passing away on November 16, 1272, after fifty-six years on the throne, Henry III was laid to rest in the abbey he built, having witnessed the birth of the parliamentary system that would outlive every royal dynasty.  De Montfort's rule ended in blood at the Battle of Evesham on August 4, 1265: nineteen-year-old Prince Edward trapped de Montfort's outnumbered army in a loop of the River Avon during a howling thunderstorm. The battle was an unchivalric slaughter: de Montfort was hacked down, his corpse castrated and mutilated, his head severed and sent to the wife of Roger Mortimer. King Henry III, who had been placed in the front line of de Montfort's army in borrowed armor, barely escaped death when his helmet was knocked off and he cried out: 'Hold, do not strike, I am Henry of Winchester, your King!' Restored to his throne, Henry ruled peacefully for his remaining seven years, passing away in November 1272. Henry III was a weak politician and a reckless spender, but his Gothic cathedral of Westminster Abbey and the parliament birthed in his turbulent reign remain the twin monuments of British civilization.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. King Henry III's Gothic masterpiece of Westminster Abbey and the parliamentary innovations of Simon de Montfort created the institutions of modern Britain. Join us next week as Rebecca returns with his formidable warrior son: King Edward I Longshanks, the Hammer of the Scots, and the conquest of Wales. Until then, stay curious.
